chunks: What is atomic layer deposition?. The question: What is atomic layer deposition?
Atomic layer deposition, or ALD, grows a thin coating (film) one atomic layer at a time. Two gases take turns entering the chamber.
Each one reacts only with the surface and stops when every spot is used. One full cycle adds about 0. 1 nm, so you control thickness by counting cycles.
The film comes out perfectly even, even inside deep, narrow holes. The cost is that it is slow.
Picture a theater with a fixed number of seats. However many people arrive, once every seat is taken, nobody else can sit.
Each round fills exactly one full layer of seats and no more. Then the next group fills a different kind of seat, and so on.
The thickness grows by the same amount every round, so counting rounds tells you the thickness.
One ALD cycle. The two reactants never meet in the gas phase because the purge separates them; each only reacts with the surface. Thickness increments by one GPC per loop.
Precursor: a reactive chemical gas delivered to the surface. Self-limiting: a reaction that stops once all the surface spots are used, however much gas arrives.
Purge: flushing the chamber with a gas that does not react so the two precursors never meet in the gas. Cycle: one pulse, purge, second pulse, purge.
Conformal: having the same thickness on every surface, including side walls and hole bottoms.
The classic example makes aluminum oxide. Trimethylaluminum (TMA, a gas containing aluminum) is pulsed in first and reacts until the surface is full.
After a purge, water vapor is pulsed in. It reacts and resets the surface, and then another purge follows. That is one cycle, and it adds about 0. 11 nm.
For 10 nm you need about 91 cycles. At about 4 seconds per cycle that is roughly 6 minutes.
A 100 nm film would take about 909 cycles, roughly an hour, so ALD is reserved for very thin films. That is the whole idea.
"ALD builds a film one atomic layer at a time by alternating two self-limiting surface reactions with purges in between.
For example, TMA reacts with surface hydroxyls until they're used up, then water restores the hydroxyls, adding about an angstrom per cycle.
That gives atomic-level thickness control and perfect conformality on tall 3D structures, so it's used for high-k gate dielectrics, spacers and barriers.
The trade-off is that it's slow."
